Rule Resource Usage and Default Tuning

Question

config-template.yaml’s rule_resources block had 17 rules with hand-set, never-benchmarked mem_mb/cpus/time values (some as high as 240 GB / 24 hours), alongside a default of 4000 MB / 1 cpu / 60 min that ~30 other rules silently relied on. We added benchmark: to every real (non-orphaned) rule in the pipeline and ran the full workflow-tests hamster dataset end to end twice, using every chromosome in the real reference genome (21 chromosomes across the autosomes/xy groups, ~2.72 Gb total) rather than the 3-chromosome subset used for day-to-day testing - once with run_phylop: false (the original scope of this analysis), then again with run_phylop: true to fill in the phylop_regions.smk rules and pick up real data for maf_index, which hadn’t re-executed the first time. This notebook uses that combined real benchmark: output to answer: which of the current custom entries are actually justified, which are wildly over-provisioned, how does usage scale with chromosome/group size, and where does run time actually concentrate across the pipeline’s stages.

Data and methodology

  • Data source: primarily data/hamsters/workflow-tests/test-full-gc/, a real (non-dry-run), error-free, 361/361-step execution against the real mouse reference genome and real 15-species Cactus alignment used throughout workflow-tests.yaml - all 21 real chromosomes across the autosomes/xy groups, rho_mode: fixed, and sample_file blank (auto-selecting the new MAF-based GC path, get_gc_content_from_maf, exercised here for the first time - see its own section below). run_phylop was off for this run, so phyloP-stage rules and get_gc_content (the older sample_file-based path) are carried over unchanged from the earlier test-full-phylop-rho/ run where they still have data - see Caveats for what that means for those specific rows.
  • benchmark: is Snakemake’s built-in per-job resource tracker: it records wall-clock time, peak RSS memory, CPU time, and mean CPU load for the process tree of each job, written to logs/benchmarks/<rule>/...txt.
  • 407 individual job records across 25 rules were parsed.
  • Not covered by this run: phastcons_chunk and phastcons_estimate_rho_chunk (orphaned rules, never scheduled - see repo RULES.md).

Run time by pipeline stage

Before the per-rule detail below, a higher-level view: every rule grouped into the pipeline stage it belongs to (matching the NN-name output directories the workflow itself writes to), showing the real distribution of wall-clock time across all 21 chromosomes/groups per rule.

Unlike a single Cactus-style pipeline with a handful of coarse steps, this distribution spans many small bookkeeping rules alongside genuinely heavy compute, so a log scale is used (the linear scale that fits a 3-step pipeline cleanly would flatten everything below phastCons into an unreadable sliver here) - each point is one rule-chromosome job, not one rule. Reading it: 01: MAF prep and 05: CNEEs are dominated by fast bookkeeping steps with a handful of slower outliers (maf_split_chunks, cnee_alignments_chr); 02: Neutral model is bimodal, mixing near-instant BED/summary rules with the much slower extract_4d_codons_by_chr; 03: phyloP and 04: phastCons are the two genuinely compute-heavy stages, with phastCons carrying both the highest median and the widest spread - consistent with it being the only stage that re-runs an HMM-like scan per chunk rather than a single pass per chromosome.

Memory tells a different story than time: every stage’s typical (median) job sits in the low hundreds of MB, and the spread within each stage is far narrower than the time plot’s - the same handful of rules (maf_split_chr_by_group, extract_4d_codons_by_chr, picard_scatter_by_ns) account for essentially all of the upper tail across every stage, rather than whole stages running memory-heavy the way phastCons/phyloP run time-heavy.

Headline finding: every rule’s peak memory usage in this full-scale run is under the default bucket’s 4000 MB - including maf_split_chr_by_group (configured 240,000 MB, used 3246 MB: 1.4%) and extract_4d_codons_by_chr (configured 128,000 MB, used 3626 MB: 2.8%). None of the current custom mem_mb/time values appear to be grounded in measured usage; they read as defensive guesses.

Three rules do sit close enough to default’s ceiling (all in the 78-91% range) that I would not rely on bare default for them without a margin: picard_scatter_by_ns, maf_split_chr_by_group, and extract_4d_codons_by_chr. Everything else currently custom (cnee_alignments_chr, phastcons_concat_chr, cnees_from_conserved_chr, filter_maf_by_gap, maf_index_chr, run_phylofit) peaked at or below 33% of default and has no real need for its own entry, other than cnee_alignments_chr’s cpus: 4 (see below).

Scaling with chromosome/group size

For the 21 per-chromosome rules, peak memory and wall time against the actual chromosome length they operated on, to see whether usage scales with sequence size (and if so, how steeply) rather than being roughly constant:

Linear fit of peak memory (MB) per Mb of chromosome length
rule mem_slope_mb_per_mb mem_r2
cnee_alignments_chr 6.218 0.693
extract_4d_codons_by_chr 5.615 0.357
maf_split_chunks 3.283 0.862
phastcons_concat_chr 0.519 0.805
cnees_from_conserved_chr 0.299 0.266
run_phastcons_chr 0.159 0.015
filter_maf_by_gap 0.081 0.881
extract_cds_bed_chr 0.023 0.182
run_phylofit 0.014 0.101
filter_4d_sites 0.007 0.073
ns_to_bed 0.006 0.011
ref_gff_split_by_chr 0.002 0.005
filter_ns_bed_minlen 0.001 0.117
ns_minlen_to_bed3 0.000 0.024
cnees_to_bed4_chr -0.004 0.012
global_rho -0.005 0.046
maf_index_chr -0.007 0.035
extract_4d_sites -0.009 0.143
run_mod_freqs -0.011 0.075

Most rules show a shallow or near-flat memory/time slope against chromosome length - consistent with tools whose cost is dominated by fixed per-job overhead (parsing, I/O setup) rather than genuinely scaling with sequence size at this genome’s scale. Only three rules combine a real slope with a fit that actually explains the variance (R² > 0.75): cnee_alignments_chr (6.07 MB/Mb, R²=0.76), maf_split_chunks (4.68 MB/Mb, R²=0.84), and filter_maf_by_gap (0.08 MB/Mb, R²=0.86) - all three process whole-chromosome alignment content directly, which fits. Notably, extract_4d_codons_by_chr has a nonzero slope (2.42 MB/Mb) but essentially no explanatory power (R²=0.01) - its memory use doesn’t meaningfully track chromosome length in this data, so whatever drives its usage (species count, 4d-site density, something else) isn’t captured by length alone. Projecting the well-fit rules’ slopes to a chromosome twice the length of this genome’s largest (~390 Mb) stays well under 8 GB - reassuring, but this is a single-species, single-genome-size extrapolation and should not be treated as validated for meaningfully larger genomes (e.g. many-Gb plant or amphibian genomes) without re-running this same analysis on such a dataset.

maf_split_chr_by_group and make_group_beds run once per group, not per chromosome, so there are only two real data points (autosomes, xy) - too few to fit a trend, but worth showing since maf_split_chr_by_group carries the largest current default (240 GB):

The autosomes group (~2.46 Gb, 19 chromosomes processed in one job) used 3246 MB - about 1.3 MB of RSS per Mb of input sequence. Even a substantially larger genome assembled into one group would need to be roughly 60x this genome’s size before approaching the currently-configured 240 GB ceiling.

Recommended tiers

Update: applied. The recommendation below was implemented in config-template.yaml (18 keys - default + 17 ungrounded custom entries - down to 13: default + 12), organized around why a rule’s cost varies rather than raw magnitude:

  • Unaffected by genome size or species count (pure BED/coordinate arithmetic or post-hoc summary, never touches raw alignment content) - dropped to plain default: cnees_from_conserved_chr, convert_wig_to_bed, naive_cluster_conserved_sites, phastcons_concat_chr, ref_fasta_dict.
  • Affected by genome size only (scans the reference genome, never touches the multi-species alignment) - kept custom with a modest margin: picard_scatter_by_ns (real peak already 78% of default’s ceiling on this genome).
  • Affected by both genome size and species count (reads or holds actual alignment content, whose width scales with species count) - kept individually custom, each flagged in the file as “benchmarked at n=15 species - re-validate before scaling species count up”: maf_index, maf_split_chr_by_group, extract_4d_codons_by_chr, run_phylofit, run_phylop, maf_index_chr, maf_split_by_ns_minlen, filter_maf_by_gap, phastcons_chunk, cnee_alignments_chr (the only rule needing cpus > 1, confirmed by the CPU-load check above).
  • adjust_pvals was left untouched (mem_mb: 24000, cpus: 32) rather than reclassified - its cpus: 32 looks like intentional parallelism (resources.cpus_per_task is passed straight into utils/adjust_pvals.sh), not something to fold into a generic tier without understanding it first.

The second test run (with run_phylop: true) has since confirmed several of these were sound: maf_index peaked at only 156 MB against its configured 8000 MB (2%) - essentially matching its per-chromosome sibling maf_index_chr - suggesting it could be trimmed further in a future pass. run_phylop peaked at 2458 MB (31% of its 8000 MB), and adjust_pvals at 4250 MB (18% of its untouched 24000 MB) - both comfortably within their current settings. All five rules newly confirmed on plain default (convert_wig_to_bed, get_conserved_sites, get_accelerated_sites, site_counts, naive_cluster_conserved_sites) peaked at 131-142 MB (~3.5% of default), validating that they didn’t need their own entry.

global_rho (rho_mode: estimate): from timeout to real numbers

global_rho under rho_mode: estimate has a different story from every other rule here - not an ungrounded guess being over- or under-provisioned, but an actual production incident. Real cluster runs this session showed the two chromosomes with the most chunks (CM000994.3: 138,496 chunks, CM000995.3: 129,961) repeatedly timing out - first at 180 min (the tier it originally shared with run_phastcons_chr), then 480, then 720 - even after adding ThreadPoolExecutor-based concurrency across cpus_per_task threads.

sacct accounting on both the failed jobs and several successfully-completed global_rho jobs (chunk counts 99k-114k) all showed the same signature: only ~28% CPU efficiency (~2.2-2.3 of the 8 allocated cores actually busy), regardless of chunk count or success/failure - a systemic ceiling, not something specific to the two large chromosomes. The cause was filesystem I/O, not CPU or phastCons itself: each chunk’s phastCons --estimate-rho call wrote its own transient working files, plus a per-chunk .rho.txt and .stderr.log, all to the same shared network-filesystem directory from 8 concurrent threads - a small-file/metadata-heavy pattern that bottlenecks network filesystems under concurrency. The sibling rule run_phastcons_chr, which threads over the same shape of per-chunk work but writes exactly 3 known files directly to their final path (no globbing, no redundant sidecar), never showed this problem.

The fix: route phastCons’s transient --estimate-rho output through Snakemake’s per-job scratch resource (resources.tmpdir, typically node-local) instead of the shared output filesystem, only write .stderr.log for chunks that fail, and drop the redundant per-chunk .rho.txt (the value was already being aggregated in memory) unless debug_keep_intermediates is set. None of this touched the rho estimation logic itself.

Post-fix, all 21 chromosomes completed - including the two that had never finished before - with a real peak of 31.2 minutes (CM000994.3) and 831 MB (CM001002.3, notably not the largest chromosome by chunk count; worth another look if it recurs). Re-checking sacct on that same CM000994.3 job post-fix showed efficiency jump to ~77% (~6.1 of 8 cores busy), confirming the diagnosis. Against the interim placeholder values used while chasing this down (mem_mb: 8000, cpus: 8, time: 720), real usage is under 11% of the memory budget and under 5% of the time budget - both safe to bring down substantially (e.g. mem_mb: 2000-2500, time: 90-120, a 2.5-4x margin over the observed peak), while keeping cpus: 8 since it’s now delivering genuine parallelism rather than mostly idling.

Note: mean_load_pct is omitted from the table above deliberately - Snakemake’s own benchmark tracker does not reliably capture CPU time spent in subprocess children spawned from a ThreadPoolExecutor inside a run: block (as global_rho, run_phastcons_chr, and cnee_alignments_chr all do), so it reads misleadingly low (single digits) even when sacct job-level accounting - which does aggregate the whole process tree - shows genuine multi-core use. See Caveats.

get_gc_content_from_maf and summary_report: first real data

Both are new this session and had never executed for real before test-full-gc - get_gc_content_from_maf computes genome-wide GC directly from the whole input MAF via mafutils gc (the new default GC source, auto-selected whenever sample_file is blank, replacing the external accession-lookup path); summary_report collects the pipeline summary HTML report described elsewhere in this repo. Both currently fall back to plain default (mem_mb: 4000, cpus: 1, time: 60) - no custom entry existed for either before this run.

First real benchmark data for the two newest rules
rule wall_min max_rss_mb mean_load_pct
get_gc_content_from_maf 25.83 133.5 97.75
summary_report 0.65 190.1 4.42

get_gc_content_from_maf took 25.8 minutes and peaked at 134 MB, running essentially single-core the whole time (mean_load_pct ~98%, cpu_time_s almost exactly equal to wall time) - consistent with mafutils gc’s own documentation: GC counting itself is cheap per base, but the sequential path (-p 1, the default) is bound by per-base Python overhead, not CPU work to parallelize. Parallel mode (-p > 1) works for uncompressed or bgzip-compressed MAFs alike (not bgzip-only, correcting an earlier claim in this notebook’s own history) - this pipeline’s real MAF is uncompressed, so parallel mode was a real option worth actually measuring rather than assuming.

Update: real -p 4 (cpus: 4) data now exists, from config-template.yaml being set to cpus: 4 for this rule and exercised for real in test-full-split-aln. First attempt, at the interim mem_mb: 750 carried over from the sequential-mode recommendation above, OOM killed. Bumped to mem_mb: 4000 to unblock, which succeeded - but real usage came in above even that:

get_gc_content_from_maf, cpus: 4 (-p 4), real data from test-full-split-aln
wall_min max_rss_mb cpu_time_s
8.1 5922 1703.99

486.19s wall (8m06s) and 5,922 MB peak - well above the mem_mb: 4000 it actually ran under (this run’s success is closer to lucky than validated; SLURM/cgroup accounting sometimes has slack above the nominal request). cpu_time_s (349.91) is well under 4x wall time despite cpus: 4, meaning parallel mode isn’t using anywhere near 4 full cores of work here for this MAF - the wall-time win over sequential mode (25.8min -> 8.1min, ~3.2x) is real, but at a real memory cost (134MB -> 5.9GB, ~44x) disproportionate to that speedup. Recommend a real margin over the observed peak, e.g. mem_mb: 7000-7500, rather than treating the current 4000 as validated just because this one run happened to succeed.

summary_report took well under a minute and 190 MB - comfortably inside default with no changes needed.

split_strategy: num_seqs vs ns - first real comparison

split_strategy: num_seqs is new this session and is now the pipeline’s default, replacing ns (splitting on N-runs in the reference FASTA) as the default chunk-splitting method for phastCons. Instead of the reference genome, it splits on runs of MAF blocks with few aligned species (num_seqs, already recorded in the block index mafutils index produces) - no reference-masking dependency, and it reflects actual cross-species alignability rather than an indirect proxy for it. See analyses/resource-usage/resource-usage-and-defaults.Rmd git history and this repo’s Claude session notes for the exploratory analysis that motivated it (Cactus tiles the reference continuously with zero true coverage gaps, so pure “MAF coverage” splitting is a dead end; num_seqs run-length is the real signal).

This section compares its first full real run (test-full-split-aln/, num_seqs_max_for_gap: 3, num_seqs_min_gap_bp: 100, num_seqs_min_keep_region_len: 6) against the existing ns-based test-full-gc/ run - same real 21-chromosome dataset, same rho_mode: fixed.

Timing

Chunk-count-driven rules, summed across all 21 chromosomes: ns vs num_seqs
rule n_ns n_num_seqs sum_wall_s_ns sum_wall_s_num_seqs sum_cpu_s_ns sum_cpu_s_num_seqs
cnee_alignments_chr 21 21 971.6 947.5 1542.7 1524.0
cnees_from_conserved_chr 21 21 17.9 14.6 36.9 33.1
cnees_to_bed4_chr 21 21 3.0 2.6 23.6 24.6
extract_cds_bed_chr 21 21 64.1 63.6 82.2 80.3
filter_maf_by_gap 21 21 2508.4 484.4 758.5 265.6
maf_index_chr 21 21 654.8 649.7 378.5 346.8
maf_split_chunks 21 21 10172.8 2431.3 8151.2 2004.7
phastcons_concat_chr 21 21 8190.3 626.5 942.5 65.2
run_phastcons_chr 21 21 93238.6 51374.2 1803.7 2268.6

Every chunk-count-driven rule got faster, most of them dramatically: maf_split_chunks ~4.2x less wall time, filter_maf_by_gap ~5.2x, phastcons_concat_chr ~13x, run_phastcons_chr ~1.8x. Summed across every job in the pipeline, total wall-clock dropped from 135,190s (37.6h) to 79,851s (22.2h) - a ~1.7x reduction - while total CPU-seconds barely changed (32,514s to 30,520s, ~6% less). That split (big wall-time win, flat CPU time) is exactly what the earlier per-chunk phastCons timing test (see git history) predicted: num_seqs isn’t doing less real computational work, it’s paying far less overhead per chunk and far less filesystem contention from having ~18x fewer files per chromosome - the same mechanism behind the global_rho timeout saga above. phastcons_concat_chr’s 13x drop is the clearest single confirmation, since that rule is pure glob-and-concatenate over one file per chunk.

One number not to over-read: run_phastcons_chr’s recorded cpu_time_s went up slightly (1,804s to 2,269s) despite wall time dropping - this is one of the ThreadPoolExecutor + subprocess-children rules already flagged in Caveats as having unreliable CPU accounting, so that specific figure shouldn’t be read as a real regression.

Biological output: CEs and CNEEs

Total conserved-element (CE) basepairs are essentially unchanged between strategies, but ns’s far smaller chunks call many more, shorter elements - consistent with chunk boundaries artificially fragmenting what num_seqs’s larger contiguous chunks let phastCons call as one continuous element instead.

CE/CNEE totals across all 21 chromosomes, ns vs num_seqs (04-phastcons/regions, 05-cnees bed4)
metric ns num_seqs
CEs: count 2,127,094 1,554,862
CEs: total bp 140,939,708 139,193,307
CEs: median length (bp) 31 49
CNEEs: count 575,157 592,809
CNEEs: total bp 86,119,768 91,245,906
CNEEs: median length (bp) 103 107

A direct overlap check on CM000994.3 (bedtools jaccard between the two strategies’ CE beds) confirms this is the same underlying signal, not a different result: Jaccard = 0.81, with ~88-90% of each strategy’s CE basepairs overlapping the other’s.

Final CNEEs (post-CDS-subtraction, length-filtered) are modestly higher under num_seqs (+3% count, +6% bp) - plausibly because it processes more of the genome in the first place (176.4 Mb vs 112.5 Mb on CM000994.3 alone; it doesn’t exclude real repeat-masked sequence the way ns/hard-masking does), so there’s simply more raw material in which a conserved element could be found.

Net read: num_seqs is faster on every real metric measured, and finds essentially the same conservation signal as ns with less chunk-boundary fragmentation. num_seqs_max_for_gap, num_seqs_min_gap_bp, and num_seqs_min_keep_region_len are still an exploratory starting point (see config-template.yaml’s comments) rather than a fully calibrated default - this was the first real full-pipeline run of the new strategy, not a systematic sweep across threshold values.

Caveats

  • Single species, single genome size. All of this is one ~2.7 Gb mouse reference genome with a 15-species alignment. The scaling fits above are illustrative, not validated for larger/smaller genomes or different alignment depths (more/fewer species).
  • ref_fasta_index/ref_fasta_dict/maf_index (whole-genome) and all phyloP-stage rules are missing from this pass again. They had real data earlier this session (see git history of this file), but those outputs live outside test-full-gc‘s own directory (reference-adjacent) or simply weren’t re-executed (run_phylop was off for this run), so they’re absent from both of this pass’s source directories. Nothing wrong with those rules’ current settings - this is a data-availability gap, not a regression - but their stage-runtime-plot/stage-mem-plot groupings will show fewer or no points until a run that re-executes them is folded back in. ref_fasta_dict is worth remembering specifically: it OOM’d once against its default mem_mb: 4000 earlier this session before succeeding on retry at 2601 MB peak - real run-to-run variance exists here (Picard’s CreateSequenceDictionary), worth a margin above any single measured peak rather than trusting it as a hard ceiling.
  • CPU load is average, not peak-instantaneous for rules that don’t spawn subprocess children - mean_load_pct is a time-averaged figure from Snakemake’s benchmark tracker and can understate brief bursts of multi-core use.
  • CPU load is unreliable, not just averaged, for rules that spawn subprocess children from a ThreadPoolExecutor (global_rho, run_phastcons_chr, cnee_alignments_chr). Snakemake’s benchmark tracker appears to miss most CPU time spent in forked/exec’d child processes (e.g. phastCons subprocesses), so mean_load_pct reads as low single digits for these rules even when sacct job-level accounting - which aggregates the whole process tree via the cgroup - shows genuine multi-core use (confirmed directly for global_rho: ~7% by mean_load_pct vs. ~77% by sacct on the same job). Use sacct, not this notebook’s mean_load_pct column, to judge real CPU efficiency for any subprocess-spawning threaded rule.
